Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization:
Teacher in Prompts, Not Gradients

Byung-Kwan Lee†, Ximing Lu, Shizhe Diao, Minki Kang, Saurav Muralidharan, Karan Sapra,
Andrew Tao, Pavlo Molchanov, Yejin Choi, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Ryo Hachiuma Corresponding author: †Project Lead, byungkwanl@nvidia.com
Abstract

Knowledge distillation transfers a teacher’s competence to a small student but is brittle in the small-student regime: forcing the student to imitate logits from a much larger teacher concentrates it on the teacher’s sharpest modes, hurting generalization on benchmark families beyond the training corpus. Reinforcement learning (RL) avoids logit imitation by training on the student’s own rollouts. However, on questions where every rollout fails—yielding zero advantage and being silently discarded—injecting a stronger teacher’s response into the policy gradient breaks the on-policy assumption and induces drift. We introduce Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization (ZPPO), inspired by Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development, which keeps the teacher inside the prompt rather than the policy gradient. On hard questions, ZPPO constructs two reformulated prompts: a Binary Candidate-included Question (BCQ) pairs one correct teacher response with one incorrect student response as anonymized candidates the student must discriminate, and a Negative Candidate-included Question (NCQ) aggregates the student’s wrong rollouts into a single prompt to surface their shared failure modes. A prompt replay buffer recirculates each hard question until it either graduates – the student’s mean rollout accuracy on it reaches half – or is FIFO-evicted under finite capacity, amplifying BCQ and NCQ inside the student’s current zone of proximal development. On the Qwen3.5 family at four student scales (0.8B–9B) with a 27B teacher, post-trained as vision–language models and evaluated on a 31-benchmark suite (16 VLM, 10 LLM, 5 Video), ZPPO outperforms off/on-policy distillation and GRPO, with the largest gains at the smallest scale. Our project page is available at link.

1 Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) and vision–language models (VLMs) have made rapid progress [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] on broad benchmarks, with reinforcement learning post-training [5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10]. The cost of those gains, however, has scaled with the cost of the model: tens of billions of activated parameters. Nearly all of the gains we see at the frontier do not transport to the regime that matters for deployment on mobile phones, AR/VR glasses, or embodied robots [11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16], where compute and memory budgets are much smaller.

Closing this deployment gap requires small models that generalize broadly, not narrow specialists. The standard knowledge-transfer recipe is knowledge distillation: a small student is trained to imitate the logits, hidden states, or sampled outputs of a strong teacher [17, 18, 19, 20, 21]. Despite its effectiveness, distillation carries a structural limitation that becomes severe when the student is much smaller than the teacher. Logit imitation is, at its core, supervised fitting on the teacher’s distribution: with limited training data, students memorize teacher answers [22, 23, 24], and the limited capacity (e.g., “mode-seeking bias”) concentrates the student on the teacher’s sharpest peaks [20, 25]. The result is a student whose generalization on benchmark families beyond the training corpus is brittle, and whose responses rarely venture beyond the paths the teacher has already taken (Tab. 2).

A line of work tries to alleviate these issues by using the student’s own rollouts to conduct distillation from the teacher to the student (on-policy distillation [25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]) or by removing the external teacher and letting the student teach itself (self-distillation [32, 33, 34, 22, 35]). These reduce the teacher–student capacity gap, but they all share the same fundamental constraint: the training signal is still a logit distribution that the student must match. For 0.8B or 2B students, model capacity is too limited to absorb such a distribution broadly, and the resulting models lose generalization on benchmarks beyond the narrow training data [22, 23, 24].

A natural alternative is reinforcement learning (RL) [5, 36, 37, 8, 7, 9, 10, 38, 39, 40, 41], which avoids logit imitation entirely and trains directly on the student’s own rollouts. However, RL has its own pathology in the small-model regime: hard questions with zero successful rollouts produce zero advantage and are silently discarded, so the student never learns from the questions where it most needs help. A simple fix – using a stronger teacher’s correct response as if it were the student’s – breaks the on-policy assumption and induces policy drift, because the teacher’s response lies far outside the student’s rollout distribution. Fig. 2a summarizes these two failure modes.

In this paper, we ask a single question: how can we transfer the teacher’s knowledge to the student without ever imitating the teacher’s logits or injecting the teacher’s response directly into the student’s policy gradient? Our answer, which we call Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization (ZPPO), borrows its name from Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development [42] – the band of tasks a learner cannot yet solve alone but can solve with a small amount of guidance from a more capable peer. Concretely, ZPPO keeps the teacher only inside the prompt, never inside the student’s policy gradient (Fig. 2b,c and Fig. 3):

  • •

    For each hard question (defined as one where the student’s mean rollout accuracy is below half), we construct a reformulated prompt – a Binary Candidate-included Question (BCQ) – that appends one correct teacher response and one wrong student response as shuffled, anonymized candidates, and asks the student to solve the problem afresh while consulting them. Since the student generates its own response, its policy gradient remains on-policy at the response level.

  • •

    In parallel, we construct a Negative Candidate-included Question (NCQ) that appends all of the student’s wrong responses, explicitly shows the student that all of them are wrong, and asks for a correct answer. Within independent rollout groups, rollouts cannot “see” each other’s wrong answers; inside our training loop, NCQ is the first place at which a student’s failed attempts become collectively visible to the student, turning independent negatives into a shared signal.

  • •

    Hard questions are also pushed into a prompt replay buffer (no responses are stored). They are repeatedly sampled until they either graduate (rollout accuracy reaches half, i.e. r¯x≥0.5\bar{r}_{x}\!\geq\!0.5) or are FIFO-evicted once the buffer reaches capacity (Sec. 3.3, Appendix F.2). This focuses repeated practice precisely on prompts inside the student’s zone of proximal development.

These three components (BCQ, NCQ, and prompt replay buffer) are layered on top of GRPO [36] augmented with DAPO’s clip-higher and token-level policy gradient loss [8]. We also adopt two simple but easily mishandled recipe choices that materially affect a small model’s training dynamics: iterations per step and batch-level advantage normalization of REINFORCE++ [37], with zero-advantage groups excluded from the batch statistics. Both are low-cost, yet ablating them accounts for a sizeable fraction of the performance drop we observe, despite their simplicity.

We instantiate ZPPO on the Qwen3.5 family at four student scales – 0.8B, 2B, 4B, and 9B – with a 27B teacher [4], post-train each student as a VLM on a multimodal RL dataset of image–question pairs, and evaluate on a 3131-benchmark suite spanning 16 VLM, 10 LLM, and 5 Video benchmarks. At every scale, ZPPO outperforms (i) off- and on-policy distillation and (ii) GRPO (Fig. 1), and ablating any single component – BCQ, NCQ, or the prompt replay buffer – strictly degrades the recipe at every scale (Tab. 3, Tab. 12). The improvements are largest precisely where the small-model gap is widest – a 0.8B student gains +9.3+9.3 pp on the VLM benchmarks, while a 9B student gains +2.8+2.8 pp – and, crucially, ZPPO also improves on the LLM and Video benchmark families that lie beyond the training corpus, the very families where distillation hurts.

2 Related Work

Three lines of work bear on ZPPO. Knowledge distillation—whether off-policy, on-policy, or self-distillation [18, 21, 25, 26, 43, 32]—shares a single training signal, a logit distribution the student must match, which recent analyses show becomes brittle when the student is much smaller than the teacher, inducing memorization and mode-seeking [22, 23, 24]. RL post-training with rule-based rewards on PPO and group-relative variants [44, 36, 8, 5] has advanced reasoning, but leaves the small-student failure mode where every rollout fails and the group advantage is zero [8] unaddressed; hybrid RL++distillation fixes [45, 46] target this mode, but route teacher responses into the student’s policy gradient through an auxiliary distillation term, which can re-introduce drift. Prompt replay, curriculum, and hint scaffolding [47, 48, 49, 50, 51, 52] re-prioritize or scaffold hard questions, but each path compromises a different channel: prompt replay and curriculum [47, 48, 49] re-expose the same hard prompt without adding any new signal about why the previous attempt failed; hint methods [52] append a directional cue (without the answer) that the student tends to copy as a shortcut without necessarily internalizing why the direction is correct; and prefix methods [50, 51] insert part of the teacher’s response as a prefix into the student’s rollout: the student is trained on off-policy trajectories conditioned on teacher response. ZPPO differs from all three by moving teacher knowledge from the gradient to the prompt via two reformulations (BCQ and NCQ), so every response is sampled from the student’s own policy, with the prompt replay buffer amplifying inside the student’s zone of proximal development [42]. (see Appendix A for full version)

3 Zone of Proximal Policy Optimization

ZPPO is built on top of GRPO [36]. We first set up notation and identify the precise failure mode that motivates ZPPO (Sec. 3.1); we then describe the two prompt reformulations BCQ and NCQ that recover a learning signal on hard questions (Sec. 3.2) and the prompt replay buffer that amplifies them (Sec. 3.3). How the reformulated rollouts plug into the training loop, together with two recipe-level choices on the backbone, is described at Sec. 4.1. The full ZPPO training step is summarized as Algorithm 1 in Appendix C.

3.1 Preliminaries: GRPO’s Failure Mode

Let xx denote a question and ySy_{\rm S} a response sampled from a student policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. For each xx we draw a group of GSG_{\rm S} student rollouts {yS(g)}g=1GS∼πθ(⋅∣x)\{y_{\rm S}^{(g)}\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm S}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x) and assign each an outcome reward r⁡(x,yS(g))∈{0,1}r(x,y_{\rm S}^{(g)})\in\{0,1\} that signals whether the final answer is correct. Let r¯x\bar{r}_{x} and stdx\mathrm{std}_{x} denote the within-group mean and standard deviation of {r⁡(x,yS(g))}g=1GS\{r(x,y_{\rm S}^{(g)})\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm S}}. The standard group-relative advantage [36, 8] is

A(g)=r⁡(x,yS(g))−r¯xstdx+ϵ.A^{(g)}\;=\;\frac{r(x,y_{\rm S}^{(g)})-\bar{r}_{x}}{\mathrm{std}_{x}+\epsilon}. (1)

Eq. (1) is the textbook group-relative advantage that ZPPO conceptually builds on; the exact estimator used in our experiments is the two-step REINFORCE++ variant of Hu [37] (Step 1 subtracts the per-group mean; Step 2 batch-normalizes across the non-trivial groups), restated in our notation as Eqs. (2)–(3) in Appendix C. The student update applies the PPO surrogate [44] on top of A(g)A^{(g)}. Either form leaves a blind spot for small students. Whenever a rollout group is all-wrong (r¯x=0\bar{r}_{x}\!=\!0) or all-correct (r¯x=1\bar{r}_{x}\!=\!1), every advantage in the group is exactly zero, so the question contributes no gradient signal at all. For a small student, the all-wrong case is exactly the set of questions that could be solved with teacher guidance. ZPPO’s goal is to recover a learning signal on those hard questions without ever placing a teacher response in the student’s gradient. We call xx a hard question when r¯x<0.5\bar{r}_{x}<0.5 and use this single threshold throughout; the cutoff is not arbitrary, since under {0,1}\{0,1\} rewards stdx\mathrm{std}_{x} is maximized at r¯x=0.5\bar{r}_{x}\!=\!0.5, where the group-relative advantage carries the strongest learning signal [7].

3.2 Prompt Reformulation: BCQ and NCQ

Both BCQ and NCQ start from a hard question xx on which we have already drawn GSG_{\rm S} student rollouts {yS(g)}g=1GS\{y_{\rm S}^{(g)}\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm S}}. In parallel, we sample GTG_{\rm T} teacher rollouts on xx from a frozen teacher policy πT\pi_{\rm T}, score them with the same outcome reward, and keep the correct ones as the pool {yT(+)}\{y_{\rm T}^{(+)}\} from which BCQ draws candidates. We use on-policy throughout in the response-level sense: every gradient-counted token is sampled from the current student. BCQ/NCQ prompts do contain teacher-derived text (correct and wrong candidate traces and, for NCQ, the parsed wrong-answer list), but this text is part of the input prompt and never enters the policy gradient as a target. Because we re-sample teacher rollouts every time xx is seen – whether new or replayed from ℬ\mathcal{B} – the candidates that BCQ uses change on every visit.

(i) Candidate compression: Before any candidate enters a prompt, the frozen teacher rewrites it into a short reasoning trace under a shared compression prompt and a shared token cap (Appendix D); the same prompt and cap are applied to teacher-correct and student-wrong traces. The rewritten text still appears only inside the prompt.

(ii) Binary Candidate-included Question (BCQ): For each hard question that admits at least one correct teacher response, BCQ uniformly samples one yT(+)y_{\rm T}^{(+)} and one wrong student rollout yS(−)y_{\rm S}^{(-)}, teacher-compresses both responses, anonymizes them inside identical <candidate> tags, randomly shuffles the order, and appends the result to xx together with a single instruction (the verbatim code-side template, including the per-candidate <candidate> blocks, is reproduced in Appendix D.1):

The student then samples a new rollout group {yBCQ(g)}g=1GS∼πθ(⋅∣xBCQ)\{y_{\rm BCQ}^{(g)}\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm S}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{\rm BCQ}) from the reformulated prompt; every response token is generated by the current student, so the policy gradient remains on-policy. The pedagogical effect comes from placing a correct teacher response and a wrong student response side by side – anonymized, shuffled, and presented without a correctness label – so the student is trained to select and reason between the two candidates without any explicitly labeled target entering the gradient.

(iii) Negative Candidate-included Question (NCQ): For each hard question, NCQ collects every wrong student rollout yS(−)y_{\rm S}^{(-)} in the current group, parses out each rollout’s final answer and lists the parsed answers explicitly inside the prompt, and appends each teacher-compressed reasoning trace as a <candidate> block, with the instruction (verbatim code-side template in Appendix D.1):

The student then samples a new rollout group {yNCQ(g)}g=1GS∼πθ(⋅∣xNCQ)\{y_{\rm NCQ}^{(g)}\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm S}}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{\rm NCQ}). As with BCQ, every yNCQ(g)y_{\rm NCQ}^{(g)} is entirely student-generated, so the policy gradient is on-policy at the response level. The pedagogical role of NCQ, however, is structurally different. In a standard rollout group, each wrong rollout contributes its own advantage to the student’s policy gradient independently, and – within independent rollout groups – the student has no way to see patterns across its failures. Within our training loop, NCQ is the first place at which independently sampled wrong rollouts on the same question converge into a single prompt: confronted with its own failed attempts, the student is cued to recognize the shared error patterns and avoid them.

3.3 Integration with Prompt Replay Buffer

The prompt replay buffer ℬ\mathcal{B} exists solely to amplify BCQ and NCQ on questions the student has not yet mastered. It stores only the question xx (image and text), never any rollout responses.

(i) Admission and graduation: After each training step we update ℬ\mathcal{B} from the current rollout batch: a question xx is admitted if its r¯x<0.5\bar{r}_{x}\!<\!0.5, and an already-admitted xx is graduated (removed) on any later step where r¯x\bar{r}_{x} reaches half (r¯x≥0.5\bar{r}_{x}\!\geq\!0.5). Because BCQ and NCQ are constructed only on hard questions, every replayed question is eligible for one or both reformulations on its next visit. The buffer therefore always tracks the student’s current zone of proximal development.

(ii) Sampling and capacity: Each rollout batch combines new questions from the data loader with replay samples drawn uniformly from ℬ\mathcal{B}, where the replay count is a fixed fraction ρreplay\rho_{\rm replay} of the new-question count. From the union of new and replayed questions, BCQ and NCQ are constructed on the hardest ones first (ranked by ascending r¯x\bar{r}_{x}); the combined BCQ+NCQ count per rollout step is then capped at a fraction ρaug\rho_{\rm aug} of the new-question count (Appendix C). The buffer therefore re-exposes each hard question many times – with freshly sampled BCQ/NCQ candidates on every visit – until it either graduates or is FIFO-evicted once |ℬ||\mathcal{B}| exceeds |ℬ|max|\mathcal{B}|_{\max}. (see Appendix C for ZPPO algorithm)

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

Students and teacher.

We instantiate ZPPO on Qwen3.5 [4] at four student scales (0.80.8B, 22B, 44B, 99B) with a 2727B teacher, post-training each student as a VLM on the ZPPO-7777K multimodal RL dataset (Appendix B).

Training pipeline.

ZPPO follows GRPO [36] with three DAPO ingredients [8]: clip-higher, token-level policy gradient loss, and removal of the KL penalty against a reference policy. We also use I=4I\!=\!4 iterations per step (vs. the standard I=16I\!=\!16) and batch-level advantage normalization [37] with zero-advantage groups excluded from the batch statistics.

Baselines.

We compare ZPPO against four families from Sec. 2. (i) Off-policy distillation (Algorithm 2): imitate fresh teacher rollouts drawn online and filtered by correctness on every step. (ii) On-policy distillation (Algorithm 3): the student samples its own response, the teacher re-scores it for target logits, and the student imitates them. (iii) GRPO (Algorithm 4): ZPPO’s pipeline without BCQ, NCQ, and the replay buffer. (iv) GRPO†: ZPPO’s pipeline without BCQ, NCQ (†{\dagger} marks prompt replay buffer). Details in Appendix D.2.

4.2 Main results

Tab. 1 (1616 VLM benchmarks) and Tab. 2 (1010 LLM and 55 Video benchmarks) report the headline comparison; 44B/99B blocks are in Tab. 10 and Tab. 11. Benchmark details are in Appendix B.2.

(i) Distillation hurts generalization beyond the training corpus. The best distillation variant stays within ∼\sim11 pp of the original on VLM, while Off- and On-Policy distillation lose accuracy on Video and degrade the LLM–Video average at every scale (Tab. 2, Tab. 11), sharpest at 0.80.8B.

(ii) Replay alone is insufficient. Adding the buffer to either distillation or GRPO yields only marginal Avg gains in Tab. 1 (+0.5+0.5/+0.4+0.4/+1.6+1.6 pp at 0.80.8B for Off-Distill, On-Distill, GRPO): re-exposure without a new learning signal does not recover the hard question loss.

(iii) ZPPO improves the macro average at every scale and benchmark family. The Avg Δ\Delta row is positive across all blocks of Tab. 1 and Tab. 2, with the largest gains where the small-student gap is widest. The buffer-isolated ZPPO−-GRPO† macro-average gain is robust to benchmark resampling, as quantified by the cluster bootstrap of Appendix F.6 (Tab. 14); this CI measures benchmark-selection robustness, not per-example or run-to-run uncertainty. Crucially, ZPPO improves generalization where distillation degrades it.

4.3 Inside the Zone: Admission to Graduation

Fig. 4 reports cumulative graduations at 22B by entry rollout accuracy, and Fig. 5 reports batch composition and graduation across all four scales.

(i) BCQ and NCQ provide a usable learning signal on the hardest questions (Fig. 4). On entries admitted at 0%0\% rollout accuracy – where ordinary RL has zero gradient signal – ZPPO graduates 28%28\% (432432/15681568) vs. GRPO†’s 4%4\% (7373/20352035); on the next-hardest, 54%54\% vs. 14%14\%. The student absorbs the reformulated signals over training.

(ii) Batch and graduation dynamics with scale (Fig. 5). Fig. 5a shows pre-cap BCQ/NCQ eligibility (Algorithm 1). BCQ requires the teacher to succeed where the student fails; as students scale up, the remaining hard questions are increasingly ones the teacher also fails on, so BCQ candidates dry up (Fig. 5a), thinning the recovery signal. In the replay buffer, small scales mostly evict before graduating, large scales mostly graduate before eviction (Fig. 5b). ZPPO’s gain is steepest where the zone of proximal development is widest. At 0.80.8B and 22B, hard questions persist long enough for BCQ and NCQ to revisit them repeatedly, compounding into the largest accumulated improvements; at 44B and 99B the same questions either graduate or rotate out before the reformulations can stack.

4.4 Component ablation

Tab. 3 isolates each ZPPO component on the 1616 VLM benchmarks (44B and 99B in Tab. 12). Starting from GRPO, we incrementally add the buffer (†{\dagger}), both reformulations together (Both = BCQ ++ NCQ), and each reformulation paired with the buffer.

(i) Each isolated component is modest. Replay alone (GRPO†) and reformulation alone (GRPO ++ Both) move only a small margin over GRPO at every scale – useful, but not sufficient.

(ii) Replay ×\times reformulation is super-additive. Pairing BCQ or NCQ with the buffer compounds far beyond the sum of isolated effects, because the buffer keeps re-exposing each hard question to a fresh candidate set per visit.

(iii) The full recipe is strongest at every scale. ZPPO ties or achieves the column max on every benchmark of Tab. 3 and Tab. 12. Within the recipe, BCQ’s contribution shrinks with scale and NCQ’s grows – mirroring Fig. 5a – so weaker students lean on the teacher candidate while stronger students lean on collective failure analysis. The same pattern holds for generalization (Appendix F.4, Tab. 13).

4.5 Additional RL recipe choices

Beyond BCQ, NCQ, and the buffer, two seemingly minor recipe choices materially shape small-student RL. We isolate them at 22B across all three benchmark groups in Fig. 6. (i) Iterations per step trade off-policy drift against rollout cost; I=4I\!=\!4 is the sweet spot. Larger II grows in-step drift: each minibatch pushes the gradient further from the current policy. GRPO’s default I=16I\!=\!16 [36, 8] runs 4×4\times as many updates as I=4I\!=\!4 but yields only a marginal gain over the original 22B base (Fig. 6a–c); I=1I\!=\!1 removes drift but undertrains at matched step count. I=4I\!=\!4 pays a small drift cost but performs four updates per step – the trade that peaks on all three (Fig. 6a–c). (ii) Excluding zero-advantage groups from batch normalization (Norm w/o Zero) is critical. Norm w/o Zero (ZPPO default) consistently beats No norm, while Norm w/ Zero clearly degrades below both (Fig. 6d–f). Both ‘Norm’ variants share REINFORCE++ two-step form [37]; they differ only in whether zero-advantage groups are used (Appendix C, Eqs. 2–3). Trivial groups (all-correct/all-wrong) carry no learning signal, but their zero advantage values shrink the batch standard deviation that normalizes every other advantage, causing inflated advantages.

4.6 Discussion and Analysis

(i) Teacher size matters: A larger teacher widens ZPPO’s gain (Fig. 7); shrinking the teacher to 44B/99B collapses the gain toward the GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!NCQ level, since BCQ requires the teacher to succeed where the student fails, and that pool of teacher-correct rollouts dries up as the teacher gets smaller. The drop is steepest at 0.80.8B, where ZPPO’s gain is most BCQ-dominated (Sec. 4.4).

(ii) Hint, Prefix vs. BCQ: We compare BCQ against two prompt-side teacher-guidance families: Hint appends an answer-free hint to the prompt; and Prefix forces a teacher response prefix into the student and lets the student generate the rest (Appendix F.5). Tab. 4 shows that Hint (Algorithm 5) helps VLM but transfers less to the LLM/Video evaluation suite, since teacher hints act as a directional shortcut without why the direction is correct; Prefix (Algorithm 6) transfers even less because the teacher prefix is off-policy, so drift accumulates over training. BCQ alone beats both because the student is trained to select between two anonymized candidates while reasoning, whereas Hint conditions the prompt on a labeled teacher-derived hint and Prefix routes a teacher-generated prefix into the response itself; full ZPPO opens the widest gap across all.

(iii) Further evidence: buffer dynamics (App. F.1), ZPPO vs. GRPO† dynamics (App. F.2), multi-metric dynamics across scales (App. F.3), the component ablation on the LLM/Video benchmarks (App. F.4), Hint/Prefix setup (App. F.5), cluster-bootstrap CIs (App. F.6), BCQ and NCQ dynamics (App. F.7), teacher capability (App. G), and compute cost (Tab. 9) are deferred to the appendix.

5 Conclusion

Distillation directly imitates teacher logits and teacher prefix-injection RL splices teacher tokens into the policy gradient, breaking the on-policy assumption and weakening generalization at small student scales. ZPPO answers our research question by keeping the teacher only inside the prompt, so the student’s gradient stays on its own rollouts while still benefiting from teacher knowledge. The flip side is a structural ceiling: questions on which both teacher and student fail admit no BCQ candidate and leave only NCQ, whose contribution alone is limited – the zone collapses to the NCQ-only regime. Extending the student’s zone beyond what the current teacher covers is, in our view, an important open problem this work leaves behind.

Limitations

Teacher-bounded zone.

The most fundamental limitation of ZPPO is the one we identify in Sec. 5: BCQ requires the teacher to succeed on a hard question, so questions on which both teacher and student fail admit no BCQ candidate and leave only NCQ, whose contribution alone is more limited (Tab. 3, Sec. 4.4). At the upper end of the student-capability range, BCQ’s contribution shrinks accordingly and the available zone effectively collapses to the NCQ-only regime. Extending the zone beyond what the current teacher covers – via curated synthetic prompts, ensembles of teachers, or curriculum-aware question selection – is, in our view, the most important open problem this work leaves behind.

Tension with dynamic sampling.

Dynamic sampling [8] simply deletes any question where the student got every rollout correct or every rollout wrong. On the other hand, ZPPO does the opposite: those all-wrong questions are exactly the ones we store in the replay buffer, so that BCQ and NCQ can rewrite the prompt and give the student a fresh chance. Hence, naively combining ZPPO and dynamic sampling is not trivial. A natural fix is to run them in sequence: first identify hard questions and only call dynamic sampling if their BCQ- and NCQ-reformulated rollouts still come back all-correct or all-wrong – that is, apply dynamic sampling on top of BCQ and NCQ. We leave this hybrid algorithm to future work.

Scope beyond reasoning correctness.

ZPPO post-trains an already-built compact VLM and is orthogonal to how such small models are first constructed – via architectural designs that compress visual–linguistic computation into small backbones [53, 54, 55, 56, 57] or via large-to-small distillation of strong teachers [58, 59, 60] – so it could in principle be stacked on any of these as a later post-training stage. Several other axes are deliberately out of scope. Extending the recipe to multi-step and agentic multimodal reasoning [61, 62, 63] is open; we neither evaluate nor train for robustness, which carries its own substantial literature on robust and causal training [64, 65, 66, 67, 68]; we do not consider inference-time efficiency techniques such as visual-token pruning [69] that are orthogonal to the training recipe; we do not target conversational or social competence [70]; we do not touch the upstream perception stacks [71] that compact models ultimately depend on for embodied deployment; and our evaluation targets single-turn reasoning accuracy rather than complementary axes such as multi-sensor perception [72], multi-turn dialogue [73], or iterative self-refinement [74]. Combining ZPPO with these complementary directions is left to future work.

Ethical Considerations

ZPPO is a post-training recipe that builds on the publicly released Qwen3.5 family (open-weight VLMs at 0.80.8B–2727B scale) [4]. We do not modify or filter the base models’ pretraining data; any social, demographic, linguistic, or modality biases present in the upstream pretraining of Qwen3.5 are inherited by the post-trained students. Our reward signal (rule-based exact-match grader plus LLM-as-a-judge for free-form questions) targets answer correctness on reasoning benchmarks, not safety, fairness, or harm reduction, so ZPPO is not a substitute for dedicated safety alignment such as RLHF, Constitutional AI, or red-teaming. Practitioners deploying ZPPO-trained checkpoints should pair them with an upstream safety alignment stage and downstream content moderation appropriate to the deployment domain. Beyond inherited pretraining bias, dataset-level bias and spurious visual–linguistic correlations are a distinct concern for multimodal models, addressed by debiasing and causal approaches [75, 76]; ZPPO’s correctness-only reward neither introduces nor corrects such biases, so these directions remain complementary to our recipe.

Appendix A Full Related Work

This appendix expands the condensed discussion in Sec. 2 into the three full paragraphs that motivate ZPPO.

Knowledge distillation for LLMs and VLMs.

The dominant recipe for transferring a stronger model’s competence to a smaller one is knowledge distillation, which trains the student to imitate the teacher’s logits, hidden states, or sampled outputs [18]. In off-policy distillation, the target sequence is fixed – a ground-truth response [17, 19] or a teacher rollout – and the student is trained to match the teacher’s per-token logits, with recent variants adaptively scheduling student-generated outputs to balance the training-inference mismatch [21]. In on-policy distillation, the student instead samples its own response during training, that sequence is fed back into the teacher to obtain target logits, and the student is trained to match them [20, 25, 26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31]. Self-distillation removes the external teacher, instead using the student itself as the imitation target – either via best-of-NN rejection sampling on its own rollouts [43, 77], or by conditioning the same model on privileged information (e.g., demonstrations, verified traces, or environment feedback) to act as an in-context self-teacher [32, 33, 34, 35, 22]. All three families lean on the same training signal, a logit distribution the student must match, and a recent line of analyses shows that this signal turns brittle once the student is much smaller than the teacher: the student memorizes, mode-seeks, or loses general capability beyond the training data [22, 23, 24]. ZPPO leaves this regime altogether. The teacher never enters the student’s policy gradient and shows up only as a candidate inside the prompt.

Reinforcement learning post-training for reasoning.

RL post-training built on PPO [44] and group-relative variants such as GRPO [36] and DAPO [8] has, with rule-based rewards, pushed reasoning on math, science, and broad knowledge tasks [5, 6, 7, 9, 10, 38, 39, 37, 40, 41], and the same recipe extends to multimodal reasoning on image–question pairs [78, 79, 80, 81, 82, 83, 84]. A complementary line scales RL compute either by prolonging training steps or by broadening rollouts per prompt to extend exploration [38, 39], regulates entropy to prevent the policy from collapsing onto its current peaks [85, 86], and probes whether RL extends a model’s reasoning frontier or merely sharpens what the model already knows [87]. However, these advances do not solve the small student failure mode on questions where the student’s every rollout still fails, the group advantage stays zero, and the question is silently filtered out as a zero-advantage sample [8]. The natural fix – replacing a failed student rollout with a teacher’s correct response inside the policy gradient – breaks the on-policy assumption and induces severe policy drift; recent hybrid RL++distillation lines [45, 46] keep the teacher in the policy gradient and therefore inherit the same brittleness. ZPPO instead moves teacher knowledge from the gradient to the prompt: BCQ and NCQ inject teacher and self-generated candidates as reformulated prompts on those same hard questions, so every response token that enters the policy gradient is student-generated (on-policy at the response level).

Prompt replay, curriculum, and hint scaffolding for RL.

A growing body of work re-introduces previously seen questions or rollouts in the spirit of classical experience replay [47, 48, 88, 89, 90], or arranges questions by difficulty from easy to hard [49, 91]. Both lines re-prioritize hard questions but neither provides the guidance that distinguishes Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development [42] from mere difficulty ordering. A complementary line scaffolds the student through difficult problems by injecting hints: prefix-based methods seed a partial reasoning trace into the response so the rollout is part teacher and the policy gradient is no longer strictly on-policy [50, 51, 92], while prompt-injected hints add pre-authored guidance to the prompt only, keeping the response on-policy and optionally correcting the resulting off-policy bias by importance sampling [52, 93]. ZPPO is also a prompt-side method on the same hard questions, but its in-prompt content is BCQ and NCQ candidates assembled at training time from the current rollout batch – not pre-authored hint text – so candidates change dynamically as fresh rollouts are sampled throughout training, with the prompt replay buffer existing solely to amplify these reformulated prompts on questions inside the student’s current zone of proximal development.

Appendix B Training Dataset and Benchmarks

B.1 ZPPO-77K training corpus

ZPPO-77K, the multimodal RL training corpus used throughout the paper, contains ∼\sim7777K (ximage,xtext,a⋆)(x_{\rm image},x_{\rm text},a^{\star}) triples — where ximagex_{\rm image} is the input image, xtextx_{\rm text} is the text question, and a⋆a^{\star} is the short gold answer used as the rule-based reward target — assembled from two publicly released sources:

  • •

    zlab-princeton/Vero-600k [94]11 1 https://huggingface.co/datasets/zlab-princeton/Vero-600k: 3434 sub-datasets covering STEM (math, science, geometry diagrams), chart/OCR (chart, table, diagram, infographic), knowledge/recognition (general VQA), and counting/grounding/search.

  • •

    OpenDataArena/MMFineReason-SFT-586K [95]22 2 https://huggingface.co/datasets/OpenDataArena/MMFineReason-SFT-586K-Qwen3-VL-235B-Thinking: a 586586K-sample chain-of-thought VLM corpus annotated with a per-example pass_rate computed by Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking (the smaller checkpoint released alongside the 235B-distilled corpus). The dataset name retains the 235B teacher tag because the corpus is distilled from the 235B model; the pass_rate column itself, which we use for our hard-example filter below, is the 4B model’s empirical success rate on each prompt.

We split sub-datasets into two tiers by their relevance to challenging multimodal reasoning:

  • •

    Tier 1 (caps at 2,8002{,}800 samples per sub-dataset): STEM and Chart/OCR sub-datasets that are directly aligned with the reasoning content the student is asked to learn (ai2d [96], geo170k [97], geomverse [98], geoqa_plus [99], mmk12 [100], cosyn_math/chart/diagram/table [101], wemath [102], tqa [103], visualwebinstruct [104], chartqa [105], arxivqa [106]; on the MMFineReason side, MMR1 [107], Euclid [108], Geo170K, Geo3K/Geometry3K [109], mm-openr1, WeMath, VisualWebInstruct, BMMR [110], TQA, AI2D, ScienceQA [111], ViRL39K [112]).

  • •

    Tier 2 (caps at 1,4001{,}400 samples per sub-dataset): auxiliary VQA, knowledge, and counting/grounding sub-datasets (pathvqa [113], vqarad [114], raven [115], evochart [116], infographic_vqa [117], aokvqa [118], gqa [119], iconqa [120], vqav2 [121], visual7w [122], tallyqa [123], pixelreasoner [124], multihop, pixmo [125], visual_probe; MMFineReason Raven, VisualSphinx [126], PuzzleQA [127], LLaVA-CoT [128], Zebra-CoT [129]).

Cross-source duplicates (e.g. Vero’s stem-ai2d_merged and MMFineReason’s AI2D) are merged via a canonical-name map and the priority-1 source (Vero) wins. Within MMFineReason we additionally drop every example whose Qwen3-VL-4B-Thinking pass_rate>0.5>0.5 – i.e. questions the 4B annotator solves more often than not – so that the corpus is biased toward genuinely hard examples. Per-sample filters: answer length ≤512\leq 512 characters, image ≥100\geq 100 pixels in both dimensions (i.e., min⁡(h,w)≥100\min(h,w)\!\geq\!100).

B.2 Evaluation benchmarks

The 31-benchmark evaluation suite reported in the main paper consists of 16 VLM benchmarks, 10 LLM benchmarks, and 5 Video benchmarks. Tab. 5, Tab. 6, and Tab. 7 list the abbreviation used throughout the main-paper tables, the full benchmark name, the scoring protocol, and the HuggingFace data source. In the scoring column, Exact+Judge first applies exact/rule matching and falls back to the shared LLM-as-a-judge only on unresolved rows; Rule+Judge uses a benchmark-specific deterministic parser before the same fallback; Det. uses a deterministic official metric with no LLM-as-a-judge; and BenchJudge uses a benchmark-specific official judge prompt.

Decoding configuration.

Training and evaluation deliberately use different decoding settings. Training-time student and teacher rollouts (Appendix D.1, Tab. 8) sample at temperature=1.0, top-p=1.0 with no top-kk/penalty terms, so the policy gradient sees a high-entropy distribution and explores. Evaluation, by contrast, uses a single more deterministic configuration shared across every benchmark and every model checkpoint – temperature=0.6, top-p=0.95, top-k=20, min-p=0, presence-penalty=1.5, repetition-penalty=1.0, max-new-tokens=12288, max-model-len=262144, min-pixels=256×\times32×\times32, max-pixels=1280×\times32×\times32 – so that any difference between methods at the same student scale is attributable to training, not to evaluation hyperparameters.

Prompt and judge templates.

For every benchmark we strip all reasoning- and answer-format directives from the upstream prompt (e.g. “Think step by step” or “put your final answer within \boxed{}”) and rely on a single shared RL closer that the student is also trained against (Fig. 8):

This guarantees that the answer-extraction format used at evaluation time is the same one the policy gradient was optimized against.

For benchmarks where exact-match parsing is unsafe, we use the shared LLM-as-judge only after deterministic parsing fails (e.g. math derivations and open-ended VLM/video questions), and use benchmark-specific judge prompts for official judge-based tasks (CharXiv, MM-Vet, HLE, MultiChallenge, and MMVU). The judge model itself is the same Qwen3.5-27B-FP8 used as the teacher in training (Tab. 8, Appendix G), running on a dedicated sidecar pool at temperature=0.0, top-p=1.0, max-new-tokens=512, and parsing only a strict JSON {"verdict": "correct" | "wrong"} from the response (any malformed or out-of-vocabulary verdict is conservatively scored as 00, i.e. wrong). The same judge model, prompt, and fallback policy – including the look-inside-reasoning fallback used when a strict \boxed{} cannot be parsed – are applied identically to every method in the paper at every evaluation step, so any cross-method delta is attributable to method behaviour rather than to evaluation-protocol differences. The shared judge uses a single Jinja2 template, reproduced verbatim in Fig. 9:

The same judge configuration is used for every method in Tab. 1, Tab. 2, Tab. 3, Tab. 4, and the appendix tables.

Benchmark-specific judge prompts.

Five of our 3131 benchmarks ship their own official judge prompt that we reproduce verbatim from the upstream evaluators so our reported numbers match the published leaderboards: MM-Vet, MultiChallenge, MMVU, HLE, and CharXiv (which uses two separate templates for its Reasoning and Descriptive question types). Placeholders in {{ … }} are filled in at judge call time.

Appendix C ZPPO algorithm

Algorithm 1 summarizes one ZPPO training step. The key invariant is that every response used in the policy gradient is generated by the current student. The frozen teacher is queried only to provide prompt-side candidate text for BCQ (and to compress candidates under a shared compression prompt and token cap), so teacher-generated tokens never enter the gradient as response tokens.

ZPPO inherits its RL backbone from three lines of recent work and adds four novel components. Inherited from GRPO [36]: (G1) group-relative advantage formulation; (G2) PPO-style clipped surrogate objective. Inherited from DAPO [8]: (Da1) asymmetric clip-higher with (ϵlow,ϵhigh)=(0.20,0.28)(\epsilon_{\rm low},\epsilon_{\rm high})\!=\!(0.20,0.28); (Da2) token-level loss aggregation; (Da3) no KL penalty against a reference policy. Inherited from REINFORCE++ [37]: (R1) two-step advantage estimator (Eqs. 2–3). Our recipe choice on top of REINFORCE++: (Z0) zero-advantage-group exclusion from the batch-statistics computation in Step 2, ablated in Sec. 4.5(ii) and derived in closed form in Eqs. 4–6. ZPPO’s own contributions: (Z1) BCQ – the anonymized binary-candidate prompt reformulation that turns a hard question into a discriminative one-of-two judgment between a correct teacher trace and a wrong student trace, both compressed by the same teacher under a shared compression prompt and token cap to mitigate obvious surface cues in the discrimination; (Z2) NCQ – the collective-negative-candidate prompt reformulation that surfaces all of the student’s wrong rollouts on the same question, together with their parsed final answers, so the student must avoid the wrong rollouts it has just produced; (Z3) prompt replay buffer with hard-question admission, graduation by mean rollout accuracy, and FIFO eviction; (Z4) the super-additive combination of (Z3) with (Z1)+(Z2) that is the central empirical claim of the paper (Sec. 4.4). Algorithm 1 annotates each step with the tags above.

A few practical notes are worth pointing out. First, BCQ requires both a correct teacher rollout and a wrong student rollout to construct a candidate pair; questions on which the teacher itself fails on every yTy_{\rm T} skip BCQ for that visit and only contribute NCQ (or, if all student rollouts succeed on the second try, neither). Second, candidate compression runs in parallel with Stage 1 scoring, so it does not stall the rollout loop. Third, the teacher rollouts {yT}\{y_{\rm T}\} on a replayed question are re-sampled on every visit – the BCQ candidate seen by the student on visit kk is not the same as the one seen on visit k−1k\!-\!1, even when the underlying question is identical. This freshness is what allows the buffer to avoid degenerating into a single fixed exemplar per hard question. Fourth, only the plain student rollouts on the original xx feed buffer admission and graduation in Stage 6: the BCQ/NCQ rollouts contribute to the gradient but are skipped when computing the per-question accuracy used to decide buffer membership, so a question is judged “mastered” only when the student can solve it without candidate references. Fifth, the three groups (plain, BCQ, NCQ) on the same hard xx each have their own group identifier and are advantage-normalized independently; the plain group on xx and the reformulated groups on xBCQx_{\rm BCQ}, xNCQx_{\rm NCQ} are sampled from different prompt distributions and never share a baseline.

What counts as a “rollout step,” a “gradient update,” and a “token.”

Because ρreplay\rho_{\rm replay} and ρaug\rho_{\rm aug} are both expressed as a fraction of rollout_batch_size, the prompt counts seen by the gradient at each rollout step are additive rather than fractions of a fixed budget. One rollout step contains: (i) XnewX_{\rm new} new prompts drawn from 𝒟\mathcal{D} (over the rollout-step budget in Tab. 8, XnewX_{\rm new} alone consumes the entire ZPPO-7777K corpus in a single pass; XreplayX_{\rm replay} does not count against the dataset budget); (ii) XreplayX_{\rm replay} prompts drawn from ℬ\mathcal{B} on top of XnewX_{\rm new} with |Xreplay|=ρreplay​|Xnew||X_{\rm replay}|\!=\!\rho_{\rm replay}|X_{\rm new}|; and (iii) at most ρaug​|Xnew|\rho_{\rm aug}|X_{\rm new}| BCQ/NCQ instances after the combined post-cap of Step 5. The cap is enforced in two stages. (a) Pre-cap on base questions (Step 3 of Alg. 1): once teacher rollouts have been drawn on XhardX_{\rm hard} in Step 2, we keep the top ρaug​|Xnew|\rho_{\rm aug}|X_{\rm new}| base questions by ascending r¯x\bar{r}_{x} that admit at least one of the BCQ or NCQ branches. (b) Post-cap on combined BCQ++NCQ instances (Step 5 of Alg. 1): because each x∈Xaugprex\!\in\!X_{\rm aug}^{\rm pre} may contribute one BCQ instance (when {yT(+)}≠∅\{y_{\rm T}^{(+)}\}\!\neq\!\emptyset and {yS(−)}≠∅\{y_{\rm S}^{(-)}\}\!\neq\!\emptyset) and one NCQ instance (when {yS(−)}≠∅\{y_{\rm S}^{(-)}\}\!\neq\!\emptyset), the pre-instance count |𝒜||\mathcal{A}| can be up to twice the pre-cap; the aug_max_ratio clause in the code then prunes 𝒜\mathcal{A} as a single combined BCQ++NCQ pool (not separately per type) down to at most ρaug​|Xnew|\rho_{\rm aug}|X_{\rm new}|. Each surviving prompt – plain new, replayed, BCQ, or NCQ – carries GSG_{\rm S} rollouts, and the actual per-step prompt count enters the gradient via gradient accumulation; FLOPs in Tab. 9 are accumulated over all gradient-counted tokens (plain ++ replay ++ BCQ ++ NCQ, with the BCQ++NCQ portion respecting the augmentation cap above), with the II-update multiplier applied to each.

Two-step advantage estimator (REINFORCE++) used by ZPPO.

Eq. (1) in Sec. 3.1 is the textbook GRPO advantage that ZPPO builds on. We adopt the two-step variant of Hu [37] (their REINFORCE++, Eqs. 6–7), which decouples within-group centering from across-group normalization; for clarity, we restate it in our notation and make explicit which sub-population enters the batch statistics in Step 2. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} denote the set of groups in a mini-batch (each group gg has GSG_{\rm S} rollouts sharing a uid), and let 𝒢⋆⊆𝒢\mathcal{G}^{\star}\!\subseteq\!\mathcal{G} be the non-trivial subset, defined as those groups with stdx>0\mathrm{std}_{x}\!>\!0 (i.e. neither all-correct nor all-wrong). Step 1 subtracts the group mean,

Ax,i′(g)=r⁡(x,y(g,i))−r¯x,A^{\prime(g)}_{x,i}\;=\;r(x,y^{(g,i)})-\bar{r}_{x}, (2)

which produces A′=0A^{\prime}\!=\!0 for every rollout in a trivial (zero-advantage) group by construction. Step 2 batch-normalizes across a sub-population 𝒮⊆𝒢\mathcal{S}\!\subseteq\!\mathcal{G} of groups:

Ax,i(g)\displaystyle A^{(g)}_{x,i} =Ax,i′(g)−μ𝒮σ𝒮+ϵ,\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{A^{\prime(g)}_{x,i}-\mu_{\mathcal{S}}}{\sigma_{\mathcal{S}}+\epsilon},
μ𝒮\displaystyle\mu_{\mathcal{S}} =mean(g,i):g∈𝒮A′(g)x,i,\displaystyle\;=\;\mathrm{mean}_{(g,i):g\in\mathcal{S}}\,A^{\prime(g)}_{x,i},
σ𝒮\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathcal{S}} =std(g,i):g∈𝒮A′(g)x,i.\displaystyle\;=\;\mathrm{std}_{(g,i):g\in\mathcal{S}}\,A^{\prime(g)}_{x,i}. (3)

The three settings compared in Sec. 4.5(ii) (No norm, Norm w/o Zero, Norm w/ Zero) all perform Step 1 and differ only in 𝒮\mathcal{S} and in whether Step 2 is applied:

  • •

    No norm: Step 2 is skipped entirely, A(g)=A′(g)A^{(g)}\!=\!A^{\prime(g)} (within-group centering only); equivalent to the standard group-relative advantage of Eq. (1) up to the stdx\mathrm{std}_{x} rescaling.

  • •

    Norm w/o Zero (ZPPO default): 𝒮=𝒢⋆\mathcal{S}\!=\!\mathcal{G}^{\star}. The batch statistics in Step 2 are computed over the non-trivial groups only, and trivial groups keep A(g)=0A^{(g)}\!=\!0 (since their A′=0A^{\prime}\!=\!0 is left untouched).

  • •

    Norm w/ Zero: 𝒮=𝒢\mathcal{S}\!=\!\mathcal{G}. The batch statistics in Step 2 include every group, even the trivial ones whose A′=0A^{\prime}\!=\!0. We make the consequence quantitative. Because Step 1 centers each group to a sum of zero,

    ∑i=1GSA′(g,i)=∑i=1GS(r(g,i)−r¯g)= 0for every ​g∈𝒢,\sum_{i=1}^{G_{\rm S}}A^{\prime(g,i)}\;=\;\sum_{i=1}^{G_{\rm S}}\bigl(r^{(g,i)}-\bar{r}_{g}\bigr)\;=\;0\quad\text{for every }g\in\mathcal{G}, (4)

    the batch mean is identically zero, μ𝒢≡0\mu_{\mathcal{G}}\!\equiv\!0, irrespective of how many trivial groups the batch happens to contain. The batch standard deviation, on the other hand, is depressed by the trivial groups’ zeros. Writing fnt=|𝒢⋆|/|𝒢|f_{\rm nt}\!=\!|\mathcal{G}^{\star}|/|\mathcal{G}| and using equal group size GSG_{\rm S},

    σ𝒢2\displaystyle\sigma_{\mathcal{G}}^{2} =1|𝒢|​GS​∑g∈𝒢∑i(A′(g,i))2\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}|\,G_{\rm S}}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}}\sum_{i}\bigl(A^{\prime(g,i)}\bigr)^{2}
    =|𝒢⋆||𝒢|⋅1|𝒢⋆|​GS∑g∈𝒢⋆∑i(A′(g,i))2\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{|\mathcal{G}^{\star}|}{|\mathcal{G}|}\cdot\frac{1}{|\mathcal{G}^{\star}|\,G_{\rm S}}\sum_{g\in\mathcal{G}^{\star}}\sum_{i}\bigl(A^{\prime(g,i)}\bigr)^{2}
    =fnt​σ𝒢⋆2,\displaystyle\;=\;f_{\rm nt}\,\sigma_{\mathcal{G}^{\star}}^{2}, (5)

    so σ𝒢=fnt​σ𝒢⋆\sigma_{\mathcal{G}}=\sqrt{f_{\rm nt}}\,\sigma_{\mathcal{G}^{\star}}. Substituting into Eq. (3) gives a closed form for the resulting advantages:

    Aw/Zero(g,i)\displaystyle A^{(g,i)}_{\text{w/Zero}} =r(g,i)−r¯gfnt​σ𝒢⋆+ϵ\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{r^{(g,i)}-\bar{r}_{g}}{\sqrt{f_{\rm nt}}\,\sigma_{\mathcal{G}^{\star}}+\epsilon}
    =1fnt⋅AZPPO(g,i)(g∈𝒢⋆),\displaystyle\;=\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{f_{\rm nt}}}\cdot A^{(g,i)}_{\text{ZPPO}}\quad(g\in\mathcal{G}^{\star}),
    Aw/Zero(g,i)\displaystyle A^{(g,i)}_{\text{w/Zero}} = 0(g∉𝒢⋆).\displaystyle\;=\;0\quad(g\notin\mathcal{G}^{\star}). (6)

    Two things follow. First, trivial groups stay at A(g,i)=0A^{(g,i)}\!=\!0 exactly as under ZPPO – they receive neither a positive nor a negative gradient signal. Second, every non-trivial advantage is uniformly amplified by 1/fnt1/\sqrt{f_{\rm nt}} relative to ZPPO. When fntf_{\rm nt} becomes small – early in training, or when the student is too weak/too strong for most questions – this amplification more often pushes the importance ratio outside PPO’s [1−ϵlow,1+ϵhigh][1-\epsilon_{\rm low},1+\epsilon_{\rm high}] window and produces the visibly worse training curves reported in Sec. 4.5(ii). The role of Norm w/o Zero is therefore not to alter any group’s centered advantage A′A^{\prime}, but to estimate the normalizing σ\sigma on the sub-population 𝒢⋆\mathcal{G}^{\star} that actually carries learning signal, so that the scale of the non-trivial advantages does not depend on the trivial fraction −fnt1\!-\!f_{\rm nt}.

The implementation (Sec. D.1, advantage estimator row) registers Eqs. (2)–(3) with 𝒮=𝒢⋆\mathcal{S}\!=\!\mathcal{G}^{\star} as the ZPPO default, so all main-paper numbers use Norm w/o Zero. The change from Norm w/ Zero to Norm w/o Zero is a one-line gating on stdx>0\mathrm{std}_{x}\!>\!0 in the batch-statistics computation, with zero compute overhead.

Appendix D Hyperparameters and baseline implementations

D.1 ZPPO hyperparameters

Tab. 8 lists every hyperparameter used to produce the ZPPO numbers reported in the main paper, including the prompt replay buffer ℬ\mathcal{B} and its capacity |ℬ|max|\mathcal{B}|_{\max}. All ZPPO and baseline runs share the same hardware pool: 6464 NVIDIA H100-8080 GB GPUs, organized as 88 nodes of 88 GPUs each; on every node 66 GPUs serve student rollouts and the gradient update, and 22 GPUs serve frozen teacher rollouts, teacher-side candidate compression, and the LLM-as-a-judge, with teacher generation overlapped with student rollouts so the wall-clock per step is dominated by the student-side cost. All RL rows – GRPO, GRPO†, GRPO ++ Both (BCQ++NCQ without the buffer), GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!BCQ, GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!NCQ, the Hint and Prefix baselines, and ZPPO (which is GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!Both) – inherit every entry below; the only differences live in which student rollout source enters the gradient (Sec. D.2).

Rule-based reward grader.

The binary reward in the GRPO-backbone row of Tab. 8 is computed by a math-aware boxed grader from the mathruler.grader library. extract_boxed_content first pulls the content inside the last \boxed{…} span of the response; grade_answer then compares that content to the gold short answer a⋆a^{\star}, treating LaTeX/numerical equivalences (e.g. 1/2 vs. 0.5, \frac{1}{2} vs. 0.5) as matches. If this strict comparison fails but the response did contain a boxed span, both sides are stripped of degree (∘, \circ, \deg) and percent (%, \%) annotations and re-graded once; the reward is 11 iff either pass succeeds and 00 otherwise. Free-form questions (math derivations, OCR, open-ended VLM) instead route to the LLM-as-a-judge described next; this routing is identical across every method in Tab. 1–Tab. 4.

Parallel teacher generation.

Teacher rollouts {yT}\{y_{\rm T}\} for the BCQ pool are generated by a co-located inference engine on 22 of every 88 per-node GPUs; their wall-clock overlaps with the student rollout phase, so they do not appear on the critical path of any training step.

LLM-as-a-judge for free-form rewards.

Whenever a question’s gold answer is free-form (math derivations, OCR, open-ended VLM questions where exact-match parsing is unsafe), the binary reward is decided by the same LLM-as-a-judge configuration [154] used at evaluation (Appendix B.2). The judge runs in parallel with student rollout scoring on a sidecar inference pool and never touches the gradient. Numbers in Tab. 1–Tab. 4 use this judge identically across every method.

Candidate compression.

The frozen teacher rewrites candidate responses into concise reasoning traces whose final answers are preserved verbatim. The cap of 512512 tokens per candidate is chosen so that even an NCQ prompt carrying every wrong rollout in a group fits well below the policy’s 262262K context window, and so that BCQ candidates from the teacher and the student have comparable length. This compression runs in parallel with rollout scoring on the same teacher-side inference pool and is therefore off the gradient path. The exact teacher-side prompt is shown in Fig. 16:

Reformulated prompts (BCQ and NCQ).

The body of the paper (Sec. 3.2) already shows the BCQ and NCQ instructions in compact form. For full reproducibility, the strings below are the exact templates appended to the original question xx – preserving the literal string concatenation, including the leading blank line and the per-candidate <candidate>...</candidate> blocks. ⟨\langlecandidate⟩i{}_{i}\rangle placeholders are filled at construction time with the teacher-compressed traces produced by the prompt above.

BCQ (Fig. 17). For each hard question with at least one correct teacher rollout, we draw one yT(+)y_{\rm T}^{(+)} and one yS(−)y_{\rm S}^{(-)}, teacher-compress both, randomly shuffle the order, and append:

NCQ (Fig. 18). For each hard question with at least one wrong student rollout, we collect every wrong rollout in the current group, parse each rollout’s final boxed answer (deduplicated and joined with “, ”), teacher-compress every wrong rollout, and append:

The shared RL closer of Appendix B.2 (“You FIRST think about the reasoning process …put the final answer in \boxed{}”) is then applied on top of xBCQx_{\rm BCQ} and xNCQx_{\rm NCQ}, identical to new questions; the student therefore samples yBCQ,yNCQ∼πθ(⋅|xBCQ/NCQ)y_{\rm BCQ},y_{\rm NCQ}\!\sim\!\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\rm BCQ/NCQ}) in the same think-then-boxed format used everywhere else.

Prompt length budget and the role of dataset filtering.

Plain student rollouts use a 4,0964{,}096-token max prompt budget (Tab. 8, Rollouts row). This budget is enforced only at dataset construction time: ZPPO-77K is filtered so that every base prompt xx – the original question text plus its post-tokenization image tokens, plus the shared RL closer – fits comfortably inside 4,0964{,}096 tokens (details in Appendix B). At training time, BCQ and NCQ append additional text on top of xx: (i) the per-block instruction string and <candidate>...</candidate> tags, (ii) the parsed wrong-answer list (NCQ only), and (iii) the teacher-compressed candidate traces (each individually capped at 512512 tokens by candidate compression; see the previous paragraph). BCQ and NCQ rollouts do not apply the 4,0964{,}096-token plain-rollout cap and are bounded only by the policy’s 262262K architectural context window (the Qwen3.5 long-context backbone), so the per-block instruction, candidate traces, and parsed wrong-answer list are passed to the student without truncation.

D.2 Baseline implementations

This subsection describes the implementation of every baseline reported in Tab. 1, Tab. 2, Tab. 3, Tab. 13, and Tab. 4. All baselines share the same student initialization, the same dataset (ZPPO-77K), the same evaluation pipeline, and the same rollout-side hyperparameters (rollout batch size, GS/GTG_{\rm S}/G_{\rm T}, sequence-length budget, optimizer, schedule). The gradient-side differs by loss family: RL methods (GRPO, GRPO†, ZPPO, Hint, Prefix) split the per-step rollout batch into II equal-sized mini-batches and apply II gradient updates on the clipped surrogate (with PPO inner-epoch =1=1 so no rollout token is re-iterated), while distillation methods (Off-Distill, On-Distill) apply a single gradient update on the entire per-step rollout batch under the JSD imitation loss. Each rollout token therefore enters the gradient exactly once per rollout step under both families.

Off-policy distillation.

We instantiate the standard teacher-trajectory imitation paradigm of Hinton-style knowledge distillation [17] as adapted to sequence models by Sanh et al. [19], with two modifications motivated by the RL post-training setting: (O1) we filter the teacher’s trajectories by correctness using the same rule-based reward as ZPPO before they enter the imitation loss, instead of imitating the teacher unconditionally; (O2) we draw teacher trajectories online on every rollout step, with no precomputed pool, so that the buffer ablation in Tab. 3 is not confounded by a one-time amortized teacher pre-compute. Concretely, on every rollout step, for every prompt xx in the rollout batch – both new prompts x∈Xnewx\!\in\!X_{\rm new} and (under the † variant) replayed prompts x∈Xreplayx\!\in\!X_{\rm replay} – we draw GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4 teacher rollouts {yT(g)(x)}g=1GT∼πT(⋅|x)\{y_{\rm T}^{(g)}(x)\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm T}}\!\sim\!\pi_{\rm T}(\cdot|x) online from the frozen teacher, grade them with the same rule-based reward as ZPPO, and keep only the correct subset {yT(+,n)​(x)}n=1Nx\{y_{\rm T}^{(+,n)}(x)\}_{n=1}^{N_{x}} (≤Nx≤GT0\!\leq\!N_{x}\!\leq\!G_{\rm T}). The teacher samples for a given xx on visit kk are statistically independent of those on visit k−1k\!-\!1 (whether or not xx is replayed). In parallel we draw GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 student rollouts {yS(g)​(x)}\{y_{\rm S}^{(g)}(x)\} that are used for hard-prompt bookkeeping (and, under †, for buffer admission/graduation), but the student rollouts never enter the imitation gradient. When Nx>0N_{x}\!>\!0, we minimize the average over the NxN_{x} correct teacher targets of the per-token Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between πθ(⋅|x,yT(+,n))\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{\rm T}^{(+,n)}) and the teacher’s per-token distribution at the same prefix [17, 19, 21] – this is the standard sequence-distillation imitation loss specialized to the teacher’s correct trajectories; when Nx=0N_{x}\!=\!0 (the teacher fails on xx at this step), the question contributes no imitation loss. Optimization shares the same AdamW configuration as ZPPO. The † variant additionally maintains the prompt replay buffer ([O3]: our extension) with identical admission/graduation/eviction policies as ZPPO; because both new and replayed prompts re-draw teacher rollouts every step, Off-Distill† matches ZPPO’s teacher-freshness symmetrically on every visit. Compared to a hypothetical offline-pool variant that caches the first batch of GTG_{\rm T} teacher rollouts per xx and reuses them on every revisit, the fully online setup we adopt costs proportionally more teacher-side compute (linear in the number of rollout steps a prompt participates in), but it removes the cache-staleness confound when interpreting the buffer ablation in Tab. 3 – any gain ZPPO shows over Off-Distill† cannot be attributed to ZPPO seeing fresher teacher samples on the same hard prompt.

On-policy distillation.

We follow the on-policy distillation paradigm of Agarwal et al. [25], with a per-token Jensen–Shannon divergence (JSD) between student and teacher as the imitation loss. Specifically: (P1) the student samples its own trajectories rather than imitating teacher trajectories (the defining property of on-policy distillation); (P2) the frozen teacher rescores the student’s trajectories to produce per-token target distributions; (P3) the loss is the per-token JSD between student and teacher at the same prefix. Our only setup-specific extension is the optional buffer ([O4]) for the † variant, which is the same prompt replay buffer used by ZPPO and Off-Distill†. Concretely, for each question xx, the student first samples the full group of GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 responses {yS(g)}g=1GS∼πθ(⋅|x)\{y_{\rm S}^{(g)}\}_{g=1}^{G_{\rm S}}\!\sim\!\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x), we then forward all student responses through the frozen teacher to obtain target logits, and we minimize the per-token JSD between the student and teacher distributions on the student’s own rollouts [25, 21]. The † variant adds the prompt replay buffer in the same way as Off-Distill†.

GRPO and GRPO†.

GRPO inherits three families of components from the recent RL post-training literature, and our setup adds three minor changes. Adopted from GRPO [36]: (G1) the group-relative advantage formulation that draws GSG_{\rm S} rollouts per prompt and centers their rewards within the per-prompt group; (G2) the PPO-style clipped surrogate objective on the centered advantages. Adopted from DAPO [8]: (Da1) asymmetric clip-higher with (ϵlow,ϵhigh)=(0.20,0.28)(\epsilon_{\rm low},\epsilon_{\rm high})\!=\!(0.20,0.28); (Da2) token-level loss aggregation rather than sequence-level; (Da3) no KL penalty against a reference policy (kl_coef=0=\!0). Adopted from REINFORCE++ [37]: (R1) the two-step advantage estimator (within-group centering in Step 1 and across-group batch normalization in Step 2; see Eqs. 2–3). Our setup-specific recipe choices on top: (OG1) lower inner-iteration count I=4I\!=\!4 instead of the standard I=16I\!=\!16 (Sec. 4.5); (OG2) optional prompt replay buffer in the † variant; (OG3) exclusion of zero-advantage (all-correct or all-wrong) groups from the batch-statistics computation in Step 2 of the two-step estimator (Eqs. 2–3; ablated in Sec. 4.5(ii)). GRPO is identical to ZPPO with the BCQ, NCQ, and replay-buffer branches all disabled; GRPO† adds the buffer alone (ρreplay=0.25\rho_{\rm replay}\!=\!0.25, same admission/graduation/eviction policy as ZPPO).

Hint baseline (Tab. 4).

On each hard question, we follow Guide-GRPO [93] (with SEELE [52] as another member of the same prompt-injected hint family). As with Off-Distill above, teacher rollouts are drawn online on every step – there is no precomputed teacher pool – but only on the XaugX_{\rm aug} subset of hard prompts that the augmentation branch actually consumes (a small fraction ρaug=0.25\rho_{\rm aug}\!=\!0.25 of XnewX_{\rm new}), which keeps the teacher-side cost of Hint substantially below that of Off-Distill.

Adopted from Guide-GRPO [93]: (A1) appending a natural-language hint to the prompt as the augmentation mechanism, before any student rollout; (A2) using a frozen teacher to generate that hint from a correct teacher trace; (A3) keeping the student rollout from the hint-augmented prompt on-policy at the response-token level – the gradient is computed under πθ(⋅|xHint)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x_{\rm Hint}) with every response token sampled from the current student, identical to Guide-GRPO’s guided-rollout formulation modulo the IS ratio it adds on top; (A4) applying the hint augmentation only on hard prompts where the unguided student rollouts fail, rather than uniformly over the dataset.

Adopted from SEELE [52]: (B1) sourcing the hint material from a teacher-derived correct trace rather than from a hand-written rule or a separate hint generator (SEELE uses partial solutions; we use an answer-free summary of the same correct teacher rollout, see the hint-generation prompt below); (B2) one hint per question per rollout step, i.e. a single shared hint string for the augmented group of GSG_{\rm S} student rollouts (SEELE generates one hint per training sample per step); (B3) the hint-augmented branch is applied as an additional augmentation group on top of plain student rollouts, rather than replacing them, mirroring SEELE’s augmented-sample construction.

The goal of this baseline is to capture the prompt-side hint mechanism of Guide-GRPO (A1–A4) and SEELE (B1–B3). Algorithm 5 annotates each step with the component it inherits. Hard questions on which the teacher itself never succeeds on the GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4 online rollouts at this step (i.e. Nx=0N_{x}\!=\!0) contribute no hint group for that step: their plain student rollouts still feed buffer admission/graduation, but Algorithm 5 skips the hint-augmented branch entirely (the empirically-observed fraction of such “teacher-fails” hard questions is small at every scale, since the 2727B teacher is much stronger than the ≤9\leq\!9B students at exactly the hard prompts the student is failing on). The hint-generation prompt is shown in Fig. 19:

The generated hint hTh_{\rm T} is then appended to the question inside <hint> ⋯\cdots </hint> tags, and the student samples a new rollout group from this hint-augmented prompt. Because every response token is sampled by the current student, the gradient remains on-policy at the response-token level (the prompt is augmented with teacher-derived hint text). Unlike BCQ, however, Hint gives one-sided teacher guidance without forcing the student to discriminate between a correct and an incorrect candidate; unlike NCQ, it never exposes the student’s own collective negatives.

Prefix baseline (Tab. 4).

On each hard question, we follow BREAD [51] (with StepHint [50] as another member of the same prefix-injection family). For implementation simplicity we omit BREAD’s adaptive Episode Anchor Search (EAS) and fix the prefix at a single token fraction α=0.4\alpha\!=\!0.4 shared across all hard questions and all rollout steps; every other ingredient of BREAD (expert-trace anchor, branched rollouts, group-relative advantages, failure-conditioned application) is adopted as-is. As in Off-Distill and Hint, teacher rollouts are drawn online on every step – there is no precomputed teacher pool – and the draw happens only on the XaugX_{\rm aug} subset of hard prompts that the prefix branch actually consumes.

Adopted from BREAD [51]: (E1) the teacher-forced prefix anchor as the start of the student rollout, drawn from a correct teacher rollout sampled online on this step (BREAD’s “expert trace anchor”); (E2) the branched-rollout structure that draws GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 student continuations from the same shared anchor (x,p)(x,\,p), so all GSG_{\rm S} rollouts in the augmented group condition on the identical prefix (BREAD’s defining “branched rollouts” design); (E3) GRPO-style group-relative advantages computed over those GSG_{\rm S} branched continuations (BREAD scores the branched group exactly this way, including the same group-relative normalization that we share with ZPPO/BCQ/NCQ); (E4) failure-conditioned application – BREAD invokes prefix injection on hard prompts where the student fails unaided, and we similarly route Prefix only through the XaugX_{\rm aug} subset of hard questions selected by our ρaug\rho_{\rm aug} rule; (E5) teacher-prefix masking from the policy loss, i.e. the per-token policy-gradient summation runs over the student-continuation tokens c(g)c^{(g)} only and the teacher-forced prefix tokens pp are masked out so they cannot inherit the continuation’s advantage (this matches BREAD’s Eq. 1 in [51], whose objective sums t=1​…​|c(g)|t\!=\!1\ldots|c^{(g)}| with pp acting purely as conditioning context). Omitted for simplicity: BREAD’s Episode Anchor Search (EAS), the per-question binary search over an episode-split expert trace that picks the shortest sufficient prefix; we replace it with the fixed α=0.4\alpha\!=\!0.4 token fraction above.

Adopted from StepHint [50]: (F1) using a strong frozen teacher (rather than human annotations or a curated SFT dataset) as the source of the reasoning trace that the prefix is cut from (StepHint draws traces from DeepSeek-R1-class teachers, we draw from our 2727B Qwen3.5 teacher); (F2) truncating the trace at the initial portion of the solution and feeding only that prefix to the student (StepHint’s “initial few steps as hints”), in our case at the fixed token fraction α=0.4\alpha\!=\!0.4; (F3) selective application of the prefix-injection to a subset of training prompts rather than to the entire dataset (StepHint’s selective hinting policy).

The goal of this baseline is to capture the response-prefix mechanism of BREAD (E1–E4) and StepHint (F1–F3). Algorithm 6 annotates each step with the component it inherits. Hard questions on which the teacher itself never succeeds on the GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4 online rollouts at this step (i.e. Nx=0N_{x}\!=\!0) fall back to the plain student rollout only, exactly as in Algorithm 5. All other hyperparameters (replay buffer, GSG_{\rm S}, optimizer) are identical to ZPPO.

D.3 Compute cost per run

Tab. 9 reports per-run wall-clock time and total training FLOPs for the headline methods of the main paper across all four student scales {0.8​B,2​B,4​B,9​B}\{0.8\text{B},2\text{B},4\text{B},9\text{B}\}. Wall-clock time is the measured per-run cost under the shared hardware setup (×64\!\times\!H100-8080 GB, 88 nodes × 8\times\,8 GPUs, per-node :26\!:\!2 student/teacher split), averaged across the per-scale runs to the nearest hour. FLOPs are estimated from the algorithms in Appendix D under the standard token-level convention – 2​N2N per token for KV-cached forwards (student rollouts, teacher rollouts, teacher KL target forwards, candidate compression) and 6​N6N per token for forward+backward – with Lgen=12,288L_{\rm gen}\!=\!12{,}288 (the configured maximum response length, Tab. 8) used as a uniform upper bound across every method. RL methods (GRPO, GRPO†, ZPPO) apply the I=4I\!=\!4 inner-iteration multiplier on every rollout token that enters the gradient – including, for ZPPO, the BCQ and NCQ groups in addition to plain and replay rollouts. Distillation methods (Off-Distill, On-Distill) perform a single gradient update per rollout step (no PPO inner loop) but incur a teacher KL forward at 2​NT2N_{\rm T} per target token. Crucially, Off-Distill is fully online in our setup (Algorithm 2): no precomputed teacher pool is materialized in advance, and GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4 fresh teacher rollouts are drawn on every prompt on every step, then graded and reduced to their correct subset before entering the imitation gradient. The teacher-side FLOPs of Off-Distill therefore scale as GT⋅G_{\rm T}\!\cdot\!( total prompts the gradient sees across all steps ) rather than as a one-time amortized precompute; Off-Distill† pays the same per-step teacher cost on both new and replayed prompts, so by construction it matches ZPPO’s teacher-freshness symmetrically on every visit. The Hint and Prefix baselines (Algorithms 5 and 6) likewise draw GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4 teacher rollouts online on every step, but only on the XaugX_{\rm aug} subset of hard prompts (ρaug=0.25\rho_{\rm aug}\!=\!0.25\,of |Xnew||X_{\rm new}|), which keeps their teacher-side cost substantially below Off-Distill’s. On-Distill instead forwards every GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 student rollout through the 2727B teacher for KL targets, which dominates its FLOPs column.

Wall-clock note.

Each ZPPO run terminates after the rollout-step budget in Tab. 8 (one rollout batch per step, II gradient updates per rollout step over equal-sized mini-batches, II-times-the-rollout-step-budget gradient updates per run in total). The reported wall-clock is student-side compute bound: on every step the per-node :26\!:\!2 student/teacher split runs teacher generation, teacher-side candidate compression, and the sidecar judge in parallel with the student rollout, and the student rollout phase (longer responses, larger group size GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8) is always slower than the teacher phase (GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4), so the teacher branch fully overlaps and does not extend the critical path. FLOPs in Tab. 9 are upper-bound estimates that count every gradient-counted and generated token at the uniform configured cap Lgen=12,288L_{\rm gen}\!=\!12{,}288 tokens with the standard 6​N6N/2​N2N token-level convention, so per-method FLOPs track the algorithm-level cost (rollouts ++ gradient passes) and are insensitive to per-method variations in average actual response length.

Other rows follow from removing or replacing the BCQ/NCQ rollout and the policy gradient pass.

(i) GRPO differs from ZPPO only in disabling BCQ/NCQ; in our parallel implementation teacher generation is fully overlapped with student rollout, so the wall-clock difference between ZPPO and GRPO is essentially the cumulative cost of the BCQ/NCQ rollout phase. (ii) GRPO†, On-Distill†, Off-Distill† add the prompt replay buffer on top of their base method; the buffer contributes a small additional overhead coming from buffer admission/graduation bookkeeping plus the longer responses that hard prompts elicit. (iii) Off-policy distillation draws GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 student rollouts and GT=4G_{\rm T}\!=\!4 online teacher rollouts on every prompt every step (Algorithm 2); the teacher rollouts are graded by the rule-based reward and only their correct subset enters the imitation JSD. There is no precomputed pool to amortize this cost, so Off-Distill’s teacher-side FLOPs accumulate linearly with the number of rollout steps. The † variant inherits exactly the same per-step teacher cost on the additional ρreplay​|Xnew|\rho_{\rm replay}|X_{\rm new}| replayed prompts, so on a replayed visit Off-Distill† and ZPPO see independent, equally fresh teacher samples by construction. Teacher work is overlapped with student rollouts on the teacher-side 22-GPU-per-node pool and therefore mostly stays off the critical path, but it contributes additively to the FLOPs column; the relative ordering of Off-Distill and GRPO in Tab. 9 reflects this scaling: at the smallest student (0.80.8B) the teacher-side cost dominates and Off-Distill sits above GRPO, whereas at larger students the GRPO column grows faster because RL methods apply the I=4I\!=\!4 inner-iteration multiplier on top of the Θ⁡(N)\Theta(N) student-side per-token cost. (iv) On-policy distillation samples GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 student rollouts per question and forwards all eight through the 2727B teacher to form per-token KL targets; this makes its FLOPs substantially larger than GRPO, whose repeated logit computation is student-side only.
