Appendix F Additional empirical results

F.1 Buffer dynamics across student scales

This subsection complements Sec. 4.3 with two views of how the prompt replay buffer behaves over training at every student scale, all measured on ZPPO runs with the hyperparameters listed in Tab. 8 (Appendix D).

(1) The buffer saturates earlier at small scales. In Fig. 20 the buffer hits its capacity ceiling within ∼\sim7070 steps at 0.80.8B and within ∼\sim100100 steps at 22B; at 44B and 99B it only approaches the cap toward step 200200. The reason is simple. Weak students fail more questions, so admission outruns graduation and the buffer fills almost immediately, whereas stronger students graduate at close to the admission rate and fill it more slowly. Either way, every scale ends training near capacity, which is the trend Fig. 5b already hinted at in the main paper.

(2) Even the hardest admission bin graduates, with the absolute count growing through 44B and the relative share rising monotonically up to 44B before saturating. Fig. 21 (left) shows that the count of graduations from the 00% admission bin (the bin where ordinary RL has zero gradient signal because every rollout fails) follows 293293 →\to 432432 →\to 562562 →\to 514514 across 0.80.8/22/44/99B, peaking at 44B and dipping slightly at 99B as the saturated student needs fewer hard-question graduations to begin with. The 00% share of the per-scale graduate composition (right panel) tracks the same shape, climbing 1313% →\to 1616% →\to 2121% and then holding flat at 2121% from 44B to 99B. In short, BCQ and NCQ supply usable learning signal on exactly the questions where ordinary RL stalls, which is the mechanism the main paper invokes for Fig. 4.

F.2 ZPPO vs. GRPO† training dynamics at 22B

This subsection isolates the source of ZPPO’s advantage over GRPO† at 22B by tracking the optimization-side and buffer-side dynamics of the two runs side-by-side.

(1) ZPPO sustains a higher fraction of positive advantages. Fig. 22 (center) shows the fraction of student rollouts with positive group-relative advantage staying ∼\sim33 pp above GRPO† throughout training. The mechanism is direct: BCQ turns an all-wrong group (zero gradient signal) into a mixed group as soon as one BCQ rollout is correct, and NCQ exposes the diversity inside an all-wrong group once at least two distinct failure modes appear. ZPPO therefore earns positive advantages on a subset of groups that would give none under GRPO†.

(2) The student stays exploratory for longer. Fig. 22 (right) shows actor entropy under ZPPO climbing to 1.21.2 nats by step 200200 vs. GRPO†’s ∼\sim0.950.95, and rising rather than collapsing. We attribute this to the buffer: its continual re-admission of hard questions keeps slowing the policy’s concentration onto the easy distribution that GRPO† converges toward.

(3) ZPPO almost doubles the graduation rate at matched buffer policy. Fig. 23 compares the fate of every entry that has left the buffer by the end of training, at 22B and at matched buffer policy. ZPPO graduates 2,6272{,}627 entries and evicts 7,2517{,}251 (26.626.6% / 73.473.4%); GRPO† graduates 1,4401{,}440 and evicts 8,6478{,}647 (14.314.3% / 85.785.7%). The buffer policy (admission threshold, graduation threshold, capacity, FIFO eviction rule) is identical in both runs; the admitted cohorts themselves differ per run, since each run only admits questions on which its own plain rollouts fail. The comparison is therefore “under matched buffer policy, what fraction of the admitted cohort ultimately graduates,” not “on the same set of questions, who graduates more.” Read that way, the ∼\sim×1.9\!\times graduation rate points squarely at the reformulation channel (BCQ/NCQ) as the thing that separates the two runs.

(4) ZPPO’s extra graduations concentrate in the hardest admission bins. Fig. 24 (left two panels) shows that under matched buffer policy, ZPPO produces 432432 vs. 7373 graduations from the 00% admission bin and 510510 vs. 169169 from the 12.512.5% bin (each run measured over its own admitted cohort, as in finding (3)). The right two panels further decompose, by number of re-sample attempts, where in the buffer entries end up: under ZPPO the “never improved” (gray) fraction shrinks monotonically with attempts and the “graduated” (dark green) fraction climbs to ∼\sim5656% by attempt 66+, while under GRPO† a stubborn gray ceiling persists. So BCQ and NCQ are turning visit time into graduations rather than into wasted re-rollouts.

F.3 Multi-metric dynamics across scales

Fig. 25 aggregates six per-step metrics for the ZPPO runs across 0.80.8/22/44/99B student scales. Three observations link these dynamics back to the main-paper claims.

(1) BCQ accuracy rises with training at every scale. BCQ accuracy starts low at every scale and climbs to a scale-dependent convergence-regime value (Sec. F.7). That rise is exactly what we would expect if the student is learning to single out the correct anonymized candidate: candidate compression matches the length and format of the two options, so obvious surface tells (preferring the longer trace, say) are gone.

(2) NCQ accuracy rises at 22/44/99B but is essentially flat at 0.80.8B. On NCQ, the student must reason about why a set of its own previous attempts were all wrong; the 0.80.8B model has limited capacity to discriminate among its own failure modes and therefore gains little from being shown them collectively. This is the underlying mechanism of the NCQ-at-0.80.8B exception in Tab. 3 (Sec. 4.4, takeaway (iii)).

(3) Entropy diverges with scale. The 0.80.8B and 22B policies climb to ∼\sim1.01.0/1.21.2 nats by step 200200 – they keep expanding their candidate distribution – while the 44B and 99B policies plateau at lower entropy after a brief rise. This matches the intuition that strong students concentrate quickly on a near-optimal solution, while weak students keep gaining from the extended exploration that BCQ/NCQ opens up.

F.4 Component ablation on the LLM and Video benchmarks

Tab. 13 mirrors the row recipe of Tab. 3 but evaluates on the 1010 LLM and 55 Video benchmarks rather than on the 1616 VLM benchmarks. Two observations carry over from the ablation. (1) Replay ×\times reformulation is super-additive on generalization too. Pairing BCQ or NCQ with the prompt replay buffer compounds far beyond the sum of the isolated effects on both LLM and Video, reproducing the pattern – the buffer’s role of re-exposing each hard question to new BCQ/NCQ candidates is not a VLM-specific phenomenon. (2) The BCQ→\rightarrowNCQ shift with scale tracks on generalization. The marginal contribution of BCQ to ZPPO’s generalization gain shrinks with scale while NCQ’s grows, mirroring the ablation in Tab. 3. Concretely, at 0.80.8B the dominant generalization gain over GRPO† comes from BCQ, while at 99B NCQ overtakes BCQ, and the full ZPPO recipe is the column-max on the macro-average of every (scale,benchmark family)(\text{scale},\text{benchmark family}) block (the original Qwen3.5 base narrowly retains the per-column lead on a handful of Video benchmarks at 44B/99B – MVBench and VMMMU at 44B, and VMME at 99B in Tab. 13).

Beyond replicating the VLM ablation pattern, Tab. 13 reveals a scale-dependent LLM-vs-VLM effect for the headline buffer-isolated comparison ZPPO −- GRPO† – the same comparison that Appendix F.6 bootstraps. From 22B onward this ZPPO −- GRPO† macro-average gap on LLM exceeds that on VLM (+3.1+3.1/+2.8+2.8/+2.6+2.6 pp on LLM vs. +2.8+2.8/+2.2+2.2/+1.6+1.6 pp on VLM at 22/44/99B), so the generalization benefit of moving the teacher into the prompt grows with student capacity. At 0.80.8B both gaps are large and comparable (+4.4+4.4 pp on LLM vs. +4.9+4.9 pp on VLM), since a multimodally-trained 0.80.8B student has substantial headroom on LLM as well as VLM.

F.5 Hint and Prefix experimental setup and results

This subsection details the implementation of the Hint and Prefix baselines reported in Tab. 4 and discusses the numerical pattern that the inline table summarizes. Hint follows the Guide-GRPO [93] / SEELE [52] family: the teacher generates an answer-free hint from a correct teacher trace, the hint is appended to the prompt inside a tag, and the student samples a fully on-policy rollout from the hint-augmented prompt. Prefix follows BREAD [51] (with StepHint [50] as another member of the same family): a correct teacher rollout is truncated to a token-fraction prefix and forced as a shared anchor for a branched group of GSG_{\rm S} student continuations, with group-relative advantages computed over the branched group. For implementation simplicity we omit BREAD’s adaptive Episode Anchor Search (EAS) and fix the prefix fraction at α=0.4\alpha\!=\!0.4. Per-step algorithm annotations are in Appendix D.2 (Algorithms 5 and 6).

Setup.

Both baselines share the prompt replay buffer (admission, graduation, and capacity identical to ZPPO), the same student initialization, the same training dataset, and the same shared training pipeline as ZPPO. Per-method compute is bounded by the GRPO†–ZPPO range reported in Tab. 9 (within the same training-budget convention), rather than listed as separate rows. Each baseline differs from ZPPO only in how it uses a teacher-correct response on hard questions:

  • •

    Hint: a single correct teacher rollout yT(+)y_{\rm T}^{(+)} is converted by the teacher into an answer-free hint and appended to the prompt inside an explicit <hint> ⋯\cdots </hint> tag. The student then samples its rollout from this hint-augmented prompt; the rollout itself is fully student-generated and the gradient is on-policy at the response-token level (the prompt is augmented with teacher-derived hint text). (Sec. D.2, “Hint baseline” for the exact prompt template.)

  • •

    Prefix: a single correct teacher rollout yT(+)y_{\rm T}^{(+)} is truncated to its first α=0.4\alpha\!=\!0.4 token-fraction and forced as a starting prefix to the student’s rollout; the student then samples its continuation autoregressively. The teacher-forced prefix tokens are masked from the policy-gradient summation following BREAD (E5 in Appendix D.2), so only the student-continuation tokens enter the gradient as targets. The remaining distinction from ZPPO is the content of the training signal: Prefix supplies only a positive continuation cue (continue a correct teacher trace), without a paired wrong candidate to discriminate against (as BCQ provides) or the student’s own collective wrong rollouts to avoid (as NCQ provides).

Neither baseline runs BCQ or NCQ. All other hyperparameters (Tab. 8) are identical to ZPPO.

Result pattern.

Tab. 4 surfaces three things at 22B that the appendix lets us interpret precisely.

(i) Hint helps a moderate amount on VLM but plateaus. GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!Hint gains +1.2+1.2 pp on VLM over GRPO†, but is still 0.40.4 pp below GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!BCQ and 1.61.6 pp below ZPPO. The student learns from teacher-side guidance, but the signal is one-sided: it never has to compare a correct teacher candidate against its own wrong candidate, and it never sees its own wrong rollouts collected as negatives. The gain therefore saturates below BCQ and the full BCQ+NCQ recipe.

(ii) Hint barely transfers to LLM or Video. GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!Hint comes in at 47.647.6 / 61.661.6 on LLM / Video, marginal versus GRPO†’s 47.347.3 / 61.961.9, because the hint acts as a directional shortcut that the student copies without internalizing why the direction is correct, and exercises neither the contrastive discrimination nor the collective-negative avoidance that BCQ and NCQ supply.

(iii) Prefix is worse on generalization. GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!Prefix loses −1.0-1.0 pp on LLM and −0.9-0.9 pp on Video relative to GRPO†, while gaining only +0.3+0.3 pp on VLM. With teacher-prefix tokens masked from the policy loss following BREAD (E5), the gradient consumes only student-generated continuation tokens, so the gap is not a gradient-side issue. The issue is what the training signal contains: Prefix supplies only a single positive continuation cue per hard question – a correct teacher trace the student copies and extends as a continuation shortcut – without any paired wrong candidate to discriminate against (as BCQ provides) or any aggregation of the student’s own collective wrong rollouts to avoid (as NCQ provides). The gain on LLM and Video benchmarks therefore lags BCQ/NCQ, since those held-out suites stress discrimination and self-correction behaviors rather than continuation from a known-good anchor.

It all comes down to the gap between the best prompt-injection baseline (Hint, 47.6/ 60.4/ 61.647.6\,/\,60.4\,/\,61.6) and full ZPPO (50.4/ 62.0/ 63.250.4\,/\,62.0\,/\,63.2): +2.8/+1.6/+1.6+2.8\,/\,+1.6\,/\,+1.6 pp. We read that gap as the empirical price of any prompt-side method that drops (i) the discriminative two-candidate construction of BCQ, where one teacher-correct trace and one student-wrong trace are anonymized and shuffled with no correctness label, and (ii) the collective-negative aggregation of NCQ, where every wrong student rollout on the same question is surfaced together. Hint gives only an answer-free guidance signal with no negative side, and Prefix forces a continuation from a single teacher trace and surfaces no negatives. Neither comes close to BCQ or NCQ on either axis.

F.6 Benchmark-selection robustness via cluster bootstrap

We complement the training runs with a benchmark-level cluster bootstrap covering every pairwise comparison reported in the main paper (Tabs. 1, 10, 2, 11, 3, 12, 13), not just the headline ZPPO −- GRPO† delta. The procedure quantifies how robust each macro-level delta is to which exact benchmarks are included in the family. For each (scale,benchmark family)(\text{scale},\text{benchmark family}) block we resample the benchmarks with replacement 10,00010{,}000 times and re-compute the macro-average delta on each resample, then report the macro-average Δ\Delta, its 95%95\% percentile CI, and the win-rate (number of benchmarks where ZPPO >> baseline). The reported Δ\Delta is this benchmark-level macro-average (the mean of the per-benchmark deltas computed from unrounded scores), so it can differ by ≤0.1{\leq}0.1 pp from the Avg-row Δ\Delta printed in the main tables, which is the difference of the rounded column averages. Within each block we draw a single shared benchmark resample per iteration that is reused across all columns and fix the RNG seed, so two columns that encode the identical comparison receive identical intervals and the cross-column deltas stay coherent. The Best non-ZPPO baseline is the strongest non-ZPPO row selected on the full sample and then bootstrapped under the same shared resample (it may be the untrained Base, e.g. on 44B/99B Video). Tab. 14 reports CIs for the main-result comparisons; Tab. 15 reports CIs for the ablation comparisons.

Scope of the CIs. Because the resampling unit is the benchmark (not the training run or the stochastic decoding seed), these CIs quantify robustness to which exact benchmarks enter the macro-average, not run-to-run training variance or per-decode sampling variance. Statements like “the CI excludes zero” below should be read as “the macro-average Δ\Delta is robust to dropping or duplicating any single benchmark in the family,” which is the appropriate stress test for benchmark-selection bias but is weaker than a statistical significance claim against training-stochasticity null.

Findings. (1) The buffer-isolated comparison ZPPO −- GRPO† has a 9595% CI that excludes zero in every one of the twelve (scale,benchmark family)(\text{scale},\text{benchmark family}) cells, with win-rate ≥8/10\geq\!8/10 in every cell and ≥9/10\geq\!9/10 in every cell except 0.80.8B LLM – the pattern we would expect if the prompt-side recipe is what drives the headline gain once all other RL knobs are held fixed. (2) The two component-isolated comparisons – ZPPO −- GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!BCQ (the NCQ marginal contribution) and ZPPO −- GRPO†+{}^{\dagger}\!+\!NCQ (the BCQ marginal contribution) – also have CIs that exclude zero in every cell, so neither reformulation channel can be dropped without giving up an empirically detectable share of the gain at the macro level under benchmark resampling. (3) The ZPPO −- Best-non-ZPPO comparison (the column-wise Δ\Delta rendered in the main and generalization tables, and the same per-cell quantity for the ablation tables even though those tables omit the Δ\Delta row) excludes zero everywhere except on Video at 44B and 99B in the main-result table, where the CIs are [−0.24,+0.90][-0.24,+0.90] and [−0.02,+0.86][-0.02,+0.86] pp respectively. The strongest column-wise baseline on those rows is the untrained base Qwen3.5 model itself, which has already saturated several Video benchmarks (ZPPO still wins on 3/53/5 and 4/54/5 Video benchmarks at 44B and 99B); ZPPO’s edge over that saturated base therefore collapses into the within-run noise on those rows, matching the few small negative entries in the Δ\Delta row of Tab. 11. Crucially, the buffer-isolated and component-isolated comparisons remain robust under benchmark resampling on these same cells, so the limitation is specifically against the saturated base Video performance rather than against any RL or distillation baseline.

F.7 BCQ and NCQ candidate-match audit

This subsection audits two distinct concerns: (a) BCQ answer-in-prompt match, that the labeled positive candidate in the BCQ prompt lets the student read off the correct answer rather than discriminate; and (b) NCQ rewriter behavior and triviality, that the rewriter quietly turns the listed wrong-student rollouts in the NCQ prompt into teacher-style correct traces, or that the student trivially picks a non-listed answer without learning to discriminate against its own negatives. We rely on the per-step BCQ/NCQ debug logs each ZPPO run writes (bcq_debug/ and ncq_debug/); the three convergence-regime snapshots per scale (the last three BCQ/NCQ-instance dumps recorded near the end of training, one per scale per branch) cover 1,5281{,}528 BCQ rollouts and 7,7207{,}720 NCQ rollouts across the four student scales. All comparisons are on the final \\backslashboxed string, normalized by lowercasing, whitespace-collapsing, and stripping \\backslashtext{...} and similar surface wrappers. Before the aggregate numbers, Figs. 26–30 walk five worked BCQ/NCQ pairs from the same logs across two outcome regimes (recovery, BCQ-only).

Setup of the worked examples.

Figs. 26–30 walk five hard ZPPO-7777K questions on which the student fails every plain rollout (r¯x=0\bar{r}_{x}\!=\!0, triggering both branches of Algorithm 1). For each question we show three things: (i) the original image, question, reference answer, and parsed plain-rollout answers; (ii) the BCQ-reformulated prompt, in which the teacher-correct trace and one student-wrong trace are teacher-compressed under a shared compression prompt and token cap, randomly shuffled, and presented as two anonymized options, plus one of the student’s GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 BCQ rollouts; (iii) the NCQ-reformulated prompt, in which all student-wrong rollouts are teacher-rewritten and listed with their parsed final answers and the student is told the answer is not one of the listed values, plus one of the student’s GS=8G_{\rm S}\!=\!8 NCQ rollouts. In both branches the gradient sees only the student’s own response tokens; the teacher-derived material lives entirely inside the prompt. Reasoning excerpts in the figures are shortened and lightly edited for length and readability (—omitted— marks removed reasoning); only the final \\backslashboxed answers are reproduced exactly. The five figures together illustrate the mechanism behind the 0%0\%-accuracy graduation result in Sec. 4.3 (Fig. 4), and two of the regimes the audit numbers in Tabs. 16–17 summarize – the recovery regime and the BCQ-only regime (0.80.8B NCQ floor) – spanning all four student scales.

Recovery regime – both branches succeed (Figs. 26–29).

Four of the five figures cover questions on which both BCQ and NCQ recover a correct rollout despite 00/88 plain accuracy. Fig. 26 (visual counting, 22B): the plain rollouts all overcount a banana bunch as 33; BCQ contrasts the uniform “each of three” trace against a per-position decomposition of which bananas are stickered, and NCQ tells the student that 33 is wrong, prompting it to name the over-counted position rather than to eliminate from a closed answer set. Fig. 27 (visual counting, 44B): plain rollouts undercount a four-spine bookshelf as three; BCQ shows the undercount against a richer colour-pattern (White, Dark, White, Dark) observation. Fig. 28 (scene QA, 22B): plain rollouts misidentify the salient attachment as either a pocket flap or a button; NCQ confronts the student with both wrong modes simultaneously. Fig. 29 (chart-reading, 99B): plain rollouts unanimously report slope 400400 mph by snapping the unlabelled half-step at x=1x\!=\!1 down to the labelled 400400-row; BCQ contrasts that 400400-row chain against one that anchors on two exact-intersection grid points and the line’s terminating arrowhead, and NCQ – where the listed wrong-rollout answers are open-ended numeric and so cannot be ruled out by elimination from a closed set – prompts the student to name the down-snapping failure mode and re-derive 500500 from positional grounding. In every case in this regime the gradient sees a positive-advantage rollout on a question that would otherwise contribute zero gradient under ordinary RL.

BCQ-only regime – the 0.80.8B NCQ floor (Fig. 30).

Fig. 30 is the cleanest qualitative instance of the scale-dependent NCQ floor that the aggregate numbers in Tab. 17 report (match-neg 82.7%82.7\% at 0.80.8B). The 0.80.8B student’s plain rollouts overlook a cluster of straws on the right edge of a pizza-meal photo and unanimously answer 00. Under BCQ the student is presented with one compressed candidate that localizes “three straws on the right edge” and another that concludes “no straws visible”; it commits to the positionally-grounded candidate on falsifiability grounds and recovers 33. Under NCQ – where the teacher trace is removed and the student is shown eight copies of its own “no straws” answer with the instruction that 00 is wrong – the 0.80.8B student fails to override its own consensus and repeats 0\boxed{0} on all eight rollouts. This is the qualitative shape of the match-neg behaviour we report aggregate at the 0.80.8B scale: the smallest student lacks the capacity to argue against its own collective negatives without a teacher-positive anchor in the prompt, so the NCQ-only signal degenerates. BCQ continues to work because the teacher trace is still inside the BCQ prompt.

BCQ audit.

For each BCQ rollout we check whether the student’s normalized \\backslashboxed string matches any positive candidate (teacher_pos_compressed), any negative candidate (student_neg_compressed), or neither. Tab. 16 breaks the result down by judge correctness. We use the table to compare two readings:

  • •

    Under a trivial answer-in-prompt match pattern, where the candidate format exposes which one is the teacher-correct trace, the student should pick the positive candidate on essentially every rollout and BCQ accuracy should approach 100%100\%.

  • •

    Under genuine binary discrimination, where the anonymized, shuffled candidates carry no obvious surface tell after compression under the shared prompt and token cap, the student should match the positive candidate on the rollouts it gets right and match a negative candidate on the rollouts it gets wrong, and BCQ accuracy should sit well below 100%100\%.

At every scale the audit favors the second reading over the first. The most direct evidence is that BCQ accuracy in the audited snapshots is 3636–69%69\%, not ∼\sim100%100\%, so the anonymization + shared-compression pipeline does not appear to leave a trivially separable surface signal that the student can read off. The within-subset breakdown tells the same story: Correct rollouts match the positive candidate 7878–91%91\% of the time and Wrong rollouts match the negative candidate 7777–97%97\% of the time, i.e. the student commits to one of the two candidates on essentially every rollout (the residual other mass is ≤22.6%\leq\!22.6\%, mostly different surface text). match-pos in the Wrong subset is ≤2.7%\leq\!2.7\% at every scale, but we note the limitation that a student that trivially aligned to the positive would by definition not appear in the Wrong subset, so this row is a weak rather than decisive signal on its own.

NCQ audit.

The NCQ prompt is constructed differently from the BCQ prompt: only the rewritten wrong student rollouts (student_neg_compressed) appear in the candidate block, together with the listed parsed final answers; the rewritten teacher rollout (teacher_pos_compressed) is logged for diagnostic purposes but never inserted into the NCQ prompt. We verified this directly on every NCQ prompt in the snapshots: 88/88 student_neg_compressed traces appear verbatim in the corresponding prompt, 00/44 teacher_pos_compressed traces appear in any prompt. The audit table for NCQ (Tab. 17) therefore changes meaning: match-neg is the rate at which the student repeats one of its own listed wrong answers (the NCQ failure mode the prompt asks it to avoid), and match-pos is the rate at which the student’s boxed string matches the rewritten teacher’s boxed string even though the teacher trace was not shown to it (the student arriving at the correct answer independently). The reading of the table is now:

  • •

    Under a trivial avoidance pattern (e.g. the rewriter compressing the listed negatives so coarsely that the student can avoid them by emitting any non-listed string), NCQ accuracy should be high but match-pos should be near zero.

  • •

    Under a rewriter-correctness pattern (the rewriter turning student_neg_compressed into a teacher-style correct trace), the prompt would now contain the answer, match-neg should drop sharply across all scales, and NCQ accuracy should be high at every scale.

The numbers are not consistent with either pattern. NCQ accuracy is intermediate and scale-dependent (1.2%1.2\% at 0.80.8B, 22%22\%/35%35\%/31%31\% at 22/44/99B). match-neg at 0.80.8B is 82.7%82.7\% – i.e. when the smallest student is given its own collected wrong rollouts and told to avoid them, it repeats one of them as its final answer most of the time. Only as the student scales up does match-neg collapse (2.2%2.2\% at 22B, 0.7%0.7\%/0.2%0.2\% at 44/99B), in lockstep with NCQ accuracy growing. This shape is what one would expect from a student that gradually learns to discriminate against its own previously listed wrong answers; it is harder to reconcile with a static avoidance pattern, where one would expect match-neg to be uniformly small from the first scale.

Caveats on the audit.

Three caveats apply to both tables. First, the comparison uses exact normalized \\backslashboxed-string match, so a student rollout that arrives at the correct answer through different surface text (e.g. “C” versus the prose description spelled out by the rewritten teacher) is counted as other rather than as a match. Second, the snapshots cover the convergence regime rather than the entire training trajectory; convergence-regime numbers do not by themselves rule out a different match pattern earlier in training, although they are the regime in which any persistent match behaviour would have had the most time to be exploited. Third, on MCQ-style benchmarks with small answer spaces, NCQ’s collective negative listing can in principle help by elimination as well as by discrimination; the audit table cannot disentangle these two contributions, and the open-ended worked examples in Figs. 26, 27, 29, and 30 (free-form counting and chart-reading, all with open-ended numeric answer spaces) are where elimination is least likely to substitute for discrimination.

Appendix G Teacher capability on the same benchmarks

This appendix focuses solely on the 2727B teacher used throughout the paper. We report its per-benchmark accuracy on the exact 1010 LLM, 1616 VLM, and 55 Video benchmarks used throughout the paper (Appendix B.2), evaluated with the same decoding settings, judges, and benchmark harness as the main-paper tables (Tab. 19–Tab. 21). The cross-teacher comparison (44B/99B/2727B teachers in Fig. 7) is presented in the body (Sec. 4.6); this appendix does not expand it. The teacher-size sweep in Fig. 7 keeps the student initialization, the ZPPO-7777K training data, the rollout-step budget, the candidate-compression prompt, and every hyperparameter in Tab. 8 identical to the 2727B-teacher headline run; only the teacher checkpoint changes between the 44B/99B/2727B variants.

G.1 ZPPO students vs. the 2727B teacher

Tab. 18 pairs every base student in the main paper with its ZPPO-trained counterpart and lines them up against the 2727B teacher; for each benchmark family we report Base, ZPPO, and the macro-average delta Δ=ZPPO−Base\Delta\!=\!\text{ZPPO}\!-\!\text{Base}.

G.2 Per-benchmark results: ZPPO students vs. the 2727B teacher

The next three tables expand both the 2727B row and the four ZPPO rows of Tab. 18 into per-benchmark numbers. All values are PASS-AT-11 accuracy under the shared evaluation harness of Appendix B.2, so the per-cell comparison between a ZPPO student and the 2727B teacher is directly meaningful.

G.3 Discussion

Two observations on the 2727B teacher link Tab. 18 and Tab. 19–Tab. 21 back to the per-benchmark structure of ZPPO’s gains.

(1) The 2727B teacher’s accuracy varies sharply across benchmarks. Even at 2727B, the teacher is far from saturated on the hard math/reasoning slices: HLE (16.016.0), OCRZH{}^{\text{ZH}} (33.533.5), BabyV (30.430.4), and OCREN{}^{\text{EN}} (55.755.7) all sit well below the macro-averages. BCQ candidates can therefore exist on hard benchmarks (HLE, BabyV, …\dots) because the teacher still occasionally solves what the student cannot, but the candidate pool is intrinsically thinner there than on saturated benchmarks (AI2D, MMLU-Rd, …\dots), and ZPPO’s gains correspondingly correlate with how often the teacher–student gap on a benchmark is non-trivial but non-empty.

(2) A ZPPO-trained 99B student approaches the 2727B teacher on several benchmarks. Per-benchmark, the 99B++ZPPO row of Tab. 19–Tab. 21 sits within ≤1.0{\leq}1.0 pp of the 2727B teacher on AIME25 (70.070.0 vs. 70.070.0), OCREN{}^{\text{EN}} (56.756.7 vs. 55.755.7), InfoVQA, MultiCh, MVerse, MVista, MM-Vet, and WeMath. We do not interpret these proximate values as the student strictly surpassing the teacher: the per-run noise band on single ZPPO runs is comparable to the residual gaps. The largest remaining gaps (HLE, VBlind, VMME) line up with benchmarks where the 2727B teacher itself is least saturated – exactly the benchmarks on which BCQ has the least leverage because the teacher cannot supply many extra solved instances the student is missing.

Putting the two together, the BCQ-pool argument can be read straight off Tab. 18–Tab. 21. Under the 2727B teacher we use throughout, ZPPO’s per-benchmark gains follow wherever the teacher–student capability gap is non-trivial but non-empty, and by 99B the student has closed in on the teacher across a good part of the suite.
